overview: The exact atlas id “south-russia” spans 1920 to 1930, but its only decoded feature is Crimea, not the Russian south. The polygon includes tested Simferopol, Sevastopol, and Kerch while excluding Rostov-on-Don, the Kuban, Donbas, Odesa, the North Caucasus, and lower Volga. Historical “South Russia” meant Pyotr Wrangel's anti-Bolshevik military government, defeated and evacuated from Crimea in November 1920; it did not rule through the mapped decade. From October 1921 the peninsula instead formed the Crimean Autonomous Soviet Socialist Republic within the Russian SFSR, then the USSR. Residents included Crimean Tatars, Russians, Ukrainians, Jews, Germans, Greeks, Armenians, Bulgarians, Karaites, Krymchaks, and others, with sharp differences among ports, steppe farms, mountain villages, and resort towns. Civil-war terror and the 1921 to 1923 famine scarred families. NEP brought partial recovery, markets, national schools, Tatarization, Jewish agricultural settlement, sanatoria, theatre, archaeology, and new infrastructure, alongside coercion and unequal access. By 1928 repression and forced collectivization were closing that opening. In 1930 the atlas wrongly recolors Crimea as “white-russia.” The Crimean ASSR continued; the seam proves neither conquest nor a modern territorial claim.

periods.title: 1920 to 1921: White defeat and Soviet violence
periods.summary: Wrangel's Government of South Russia held Crimea only until Red forces broke the Perekop defenses in November 1920. Soldiers and civilians evacuated by sea; those remaining faced screening, imprisonment, and mass execution. The atlas freezes that dying White label across a decade even though Soviet rule followed almost immediately.

periods.title: 1921 to 1922: autonomy amid famine
periods.summary: The Crimean Soviet republic was constituted inside the Russian SFSR in October 1921, not as an independent “South Russia.” War damage, requisitioning, drought, disrupted farming, and delayed recognition of catastrophe drove a devastating famine. Crimean Tatar villages and south-coast communities suffered especially, while relief arrived unevenly.

periods.title: 1922 to 1923: Union formation and survival work
periods.summary: Russia, Ukraine, Belarus, and Transcaucasia declared the USSR in December 1922; Crimea remained an autonomous republic inside the Russian member republic. American and Turkish relief networks supplied food or medicine as famine continued. Local government also announced Tatarization, tying Soviet authority to native-language administration and schooling.

periods.title: 1923 to 1924: NEP recovery and contested land
periods.summary: New Economic Policy reopened limited markets and permitted some leasing and hired labor, but land remained fiercely contested. Crimean Tatar peasants challenged south-coast state farms. In Simferopol a state Crimean Tatar drama theatre opened in 1923, showing cultural institution-building beside hunger, policing, and economic repair.

periods.title: 1924 to 1925: settlement schemes and resort experiments
periods.summary: Agro-Joint and Soviet agencies expanded plans for Jewish agricultural settlement, offering equipment, credit, agronomy, and schools while intensifying disputes over supposedly vacant land. Nationalized palaces and villas became health resorts; administrators balanced promises of worker treatment against scarce beds, political selection, cost, and self-financing.

periods.title: 1925 to 1926: camps, pipes, and rebuilding
periods.summary: Artek opened in 1925 as a small children's sanatorium camp, while Sevastopol created a water trust and Simferopol opened a sewer system. These projects were real achievements but reached selected children and uneven urban districts. Farms, vineyards, ports, workshops, and households still carried wartime losses and shortages.

periods.title: 1926 to 1927: a census reveals plurality
periods.summary: The 1926 census recorded a highly mixed peninsula and substantial literacy, with large local differences by town, countryside, language, gender, and age. National schools and publications expanded under Tatarization. Census categories help measure diversity, but they cannot turn fluid identities or multilingual households into sealed ethnic boxes.

periods.title: 1927 to 1928: earthquakes and a narrowing cultural opening
periods.summary: Two 1927 earthquakes damaged southern Crimea and prompted instrumental observation at Yalta, Feodosiia, Simferopol, and Sevastopol. Cultural institutions, schools, literature, and clothing were changing under Soviet pressure. By early 1928 arrests around Crimean Tatar leader Veli Ibrahimov signaled that Tatarization's political space was closing.

periods.title: 1928 to 1929: script reform and repression
periods.summary: Crimean Tatar print shifted from reformed Arabic writing toward a Latin alphabet in 1928, changing textbooks, newspapers, and adult learning. The same year Veli Ibrahimov was executed after a politicized case. Cultural modernization and coercive centralization therefore advanced together, while Stalin's “Great Break” prepared forced collectivization.

periods.title: 1929 to 1930: collectivization and a false map ending
periods.summary: Mass collectivization, grain procurement, and campaigns against alleged kulaks overturned the NEP rural compromise. Families faced property loss, expulsion, and sharper state control. At 1930 the atlas deletes “south-russia” and paints every sampled Soviet point “white-russia,” another cartographic error; Crimea's autonomous republic did not disappear.

sections.title: Read the atlas label as Crimea, not a southern empire

items.text: The live index contains one exact “south-russia” record named “South Russia,” approximately 1920 to 1930. One border snapshot carries it, but its researched card and override are missing. The imported summary correctly ends Wrangel's White South in 1920, so it cannot explain the atlas feature's extra decade.

The only decoded target is one Polygon with one component, one ring, 39 positions, and bbox 32.50292502925029, 44.491549258420484 to 36.520565205652076, 46.192463742475915. Its geometry SHA-256 is 27eb507d7271400ebe45a546b0d4c05d8fc1a3ff7df60e56f225f4a4bdb01824. That footprint is Crimea, not all southern Russia. It audits a simplified software shape, not a surveyed historical frontier.

Tested Simferopol, Sevastopol, and Kerch fall inside. Rostov-on-Don, Novocherkassk, Taganrog, Krasnodar, Novorossiysk, Sochi, Stavropol, Armavir, Maykop, Elista, Tsaritsyn, Astrakhan, Donetsk, Mariupol, Kharkiv, Kyiv, Odesa, Makhachkala, Grozny, and Vladikavkaz do not. The label's geographic mismatch is therefore measurable, not merely semantic.

In 1914 every tested Crimean and southern point is assigned to “russian-empire.” In 1920 only the three Crimean probes enter “south-russia”; Rostov and Krasnodar are already “ussr,” while Donetsk and Odesa are “ukraine.” The sudden categories describe atlas design, not a uniform founding, border treaty, or popular allegiance.

At 1930 the target vanishes and every sampled Soviet point, from Crimea to Moscow and Baku, is misassigned to “white-russia.” By 1938 and 1945 all tested Crimean and Soviet comparators return to “ussr.” The endpoint is a broad atlas failure, not Belarusian rule, White restoration, or Crimean collapse.

sections.title: Follow war, evacuation, terror, autonomy, and Union rule

items.text: Wrangel's Government of South Russia was a White military and civilian regime centered on Crimea during 1920, not a stable country lasting to 1930. Its archives show attempted land reform and administration under severe military pressure. Municipal politicians could oppose it, and residents were never one ideological camp.

Red forces breached Perekop in November 1920, and Wrangel ordered evacuation from Crimean ports. Ships carried soldiers, officials, families, refugees, foreign personnel, and supplies toward Constantinople. Numbers vary by source, so the card emphasizes the documented movement and separation rather than pretending that every evacuee shared one motive or fate.

After the White defeat, Soviet security organs screened prisoners and civilians and carried out mass executions from November 1920 into 1921. Archival historians debate totals and categories. The secure conclusion is organized lethal repression on a large scale; disputed numbers should never become a gruesome scoreboard or erase individual victims.

The 1921 Crimean constitution placed the republic inside the Russian SFSR. Its institutions used Soviet congresses, executive committees, and commissariats, while autonomy and Tatarization emerged through negotiation and coercion. This was neither Wrangel's government nor an independent nation-state, and constitutional words did not guarantee equal power or safety.

When the USSR was declared in December 1922, Crimea did not join as a union republic. It remained an autonomous republic within the Russian SFSR, one of the new Union's constituent republics. Moscow gained extensive federal authority, while local institutions continued under layered party and state control that residents encountered unevenly.

sections.title: Meet a multilingual peninsula and contested national policies

items.text: The 1926 census and local city studies show Crimea as multiethnic and multilingual: Crimean Tatars, Russians, Ukrainians, Jews, Germans, Greeks, Armenians, Bulgarians, Karaites, Krymchaks, and others lived in different proportions across towns and countryside. Census labels are valuable evidence, but mixed homes, changing language, migration, and self-identification resist tidy boxes.

Tatarization promoted Crimean Tatar personnel, schools, publications, and public-language use during the 1920s. It partly recognized an Indigenous population marginalized by empire and war, yet operated inside a one-party system. National institutions created real opportunities without making every Crimean Tatar supportive, every official bilingual, or every village equally served.

Veli Ibrahimov, a Crimean Tatar communist and republic leader, defended land and staffing priorities that increasingly clashed with central policy. His 1928 arrest and execution marked a decisive assault on Tatarization's leadership. Treating the case simply as factional politics would miss the fear carried into offices, schools, villages, and families.

Muslims, Orthodox Christians, Jews, Karaites, Krymchaks, Catholics, and other communities maintained worship, family rites, calendars, charity, and social networks. Soviet authorities regulated, taxed, closed, or repurposed religious institutions while promoting atheism. Practice varied by locality and generation; neither “religious Crimea” nor “atheist Crimea” describes everyone.

National village councils and schools could make language and representation visible, while settlement schemes redistributed land and resources. Jewish agricultural colonists built new cooperatives with Soviet and overseas aid; Crimean Tatar leaders protested allocations they considered unjust. Both communities had diverse interests, so conflict must not be recast as timeless ethnic hostility.

sections.title: Work farms, vineyards, ports, markets, and new settlements

items.text: Crimean agriculture differed sharply by ecology. Steppe districts emphasized grain and livestock; foothills mixed crops; mountain and south-coast zones supported orchards, vineyards, and tobacco. War, famine, animal losses, land redistribution, weather, and access to tools changed each household's choices. One peninsula-wide peasant routine would be fictional.

NEP restored limited legal trade, cooperatives, leasing, and some hired labor after War Communism, helping markets and farms recover. It did not restore prewar ownership or remove taxes and state procurement. Traders, artisans, porters, shopkeepers, seasonal workers, and farmers navigated changing rules whose enforcement differed across districts.

Ports including Feodosiia and Yevpatoriia connected shipping, fishing, military facilities, salt, grain, fruit, wine, and passengers. Rail and cart routes tied harbors to Simferopol and rural producers. Port activity also meant inspections, dangerous loading, irregular employment, and family separation, not simply bustling prosperity.

From 1924 Agro-Joint and Soviet bodies supported Jewish farming settlements with land plans, machinery, credit, agronomists, health work, and schools. Colonists had to learn unfamiliar soils and farm routines. Calling northern Crimea “empty” hides earlier users, landless Crimean Tatars, ecological limits, and political disputes over allocation.

A 1924 to 1925 Crimean budget basket lists rye and wheat flour, millet, potatoes, meat, butter, milk, vegetable oil, herring, sugar, cloth, kerosene, soap, tobacco, and firewood. It describes priced necessities for university staff, not everyone's pantry, but restores ordinary purchasing decisions to economic history.

sections.title: Enter families, homes, meals, clothes, and social life

items.text: Families absorbed demobilization, death, exile, famine, migration, unemployment, and new wage work. Adults and older children combined paid labor with cooking, fuel gathering, care, repairs, and queues. Interwar household studies reveal gendered and age-graded work, but a Soviet average cannot replace evidence for each Crimean Tatar village, port family, or settler household.

Soviet law expanded civil marriage, divorce, women's formal equality, children's legal status, and access to abortion. Those rules mattered, but paperwork, housing, income, childcare, religion, kin expectations, and local officials shaped actual choices. Legal emancipation did not wash dishes, find wages, or make an unsafe partner disappear.

Housing ranged from rural farmsteads and Crimean Tatar village homes to port rooms, divided urban apartments, barracks, sanatorium wards, and repurposed villas. Crowding and fuel shortages could turn privacy into a luxury. Evidence from Moscow hygiene campaigns is only a comparator, not permission to assign communal apartments to every Crimean household.

Meals reflected grain, potatoes, dairy, vegetables, fruit, fish, meat, oil, and local or religious practice, but access varied drastically. Contemporary price lists record goods, not what every family ate. During famine even familiar foods became unobtainable, and relief rations cannot be mistaken for a normal Crimean diet.

Clothing marked occupation, gender, age, faith, wealth, and setting. Crimean Tatar dress changed under urban fashion and Soviet campaigns, while work clothes faced salt, soil, grease, weather, and repeated mending. Photographs and costume debates preserve selected appearances; they rarely inventory the patched shirt worn to exhaustion.

sections.title: Grow up, teach, learn, and navigate changing rights

items.text: War, evacuation, famine, epidemic disease, and adult death left children hungry, displaced, or without dependable caregivers. Schools and orphanages faced overwhelming demand and weak supplies. General Soviet evidence documents institutional scarcity; Yalta evidence confirms severe local population loss. Neither source permits a precise peninsula-wide count of homeless children.

National-language schools, literacy classes, teacher training, clubs, and libraries expanded, but buildings, books, trained staff, and attendance remained uneven. Census analysis reports high Crimean literacy relative to many regions, yet urban and rural opportunity differed. Reading ability also ranged from signing a form to handling complex literature.

Crimean Tatar women worked as teachers and cultural organizers while journals debated education, consent in marriage, property, leisure, and public participation. These debates reveal women speaking and acting, not a single “traditional” position. Formal rights still met childcare burdens, poverty, patriarchal authority, state surveillance, and differences among families.

Artek opened in June 1925 as a small sanatorium camp for medically selected children. Archival files preserve selection letters, schedules, transport reports, and photographs. That evidence illuminates some children's meals, rest, outdoor routines, and supervision, but it describes an exceptional institution, not an average Crimean summer vacation.

Children learned in secular schools, Crimean Tatar institutions, families, farms, workshops, religious settings, youth groups, and workplaces. Soviet educational experiments sought mass access while teacher and orphanage shortages narrowed delivery. A timetable can show official hopes; it cannot reveal every child's fear, curiosity, chores, language switches, or missed class.

sections.title: Read law, scripts, newspapers, theatre, and archaeology

items.text: Written-language sample, Simferopol, 1924 publication of the 1921 constitution: “Конституция Крымской Советской Социалистической Республики.” Transliteration: “Konstitutsiya Krymskoy Sovetskoy Sotsialisticheskoy Respubliki.” Translation: “Constitution of the Crimean Soviet Socialist Republic.” This is a Russian legal title in Cyrillic, securely cataloged by the Presidential Library, not everyday speech.

Crimean Tatar, Russian, Ukrainian, Yiddish, German, Greek, Armenian, and other languages circulated in homes, schools, administration, worship, trade, and print. Crimean Tatar writing moved from reformed Arabic script toward Latin letters in 1928. Script reform changed literacy work and access; it did not instantly change speech or erase older readers.

The Crimean Tatar State Drama Theatre opened in Simferopol in 1923 and employed writers, actors, directors, musicians, costumers, stage workers, and ticket staff. Theatre could support language and public culture while serving Soviet institutions. A state logo never performed a play by itself; people did the rehearsing, sewing, hauling, and remembering.

The Muslim journal Asriy Musulmanliq discussed women's education, consent, property, leisure, and civic participation between 1924 and 1927. Newspapers and magazines created argument rather than automatic consensus. Editors, subscribers, teachers, religious thinkers, secular activists, and readers could disagree, and surviving print does not measure what every household believed.

Crimean archaeologists and museum workers excavated, cataloged, protected, and published sites during the 1920s, including Chersonesos. Their work preserved knowledge and trained specialists, yet institutions also fought for land, buildings, funds, and authority. Archaeology was an achievement produced by field crews and archives, and it could also serve state narratives.

sections.title: Face famine, epidemics, medicine, resorts, and earthquakes

items.text: Famine weakened bodies already affected by war, displacement, cold, and disease. Yalta histories record severe loss, while relief archives show food and medicine moving through international systems. Typhus, relapsing fever, typhoid, and other infections traveled with hunger and crowding. Survival depended on locality, timing, connections, and aid access.

The Soviet health system emphasized unified administration, prevention, vaccination, sanitation, and campaigns against tuberculosis, venereal disease, and alcoholism. These were ambitious public-health tools rather than proof of universal treatment. Clinics still needed trained staff, beds, drugs, transport, trust, clean water, and time that famine-stricken families might not have.

Sevastopol rebuilt a city health department and medical institutions after war, but shortages constrained services. Hospitals, outpatient care, sanitary work, and epidemic response reached a strategic port with unusual needs. Evidence from Sevastopol cannot represent a mountain village, and formal availability does not prove affordable, timely, or culturally trusted care.

Nationalized villas, estates, and palaces supported plans for a “workers' health resort.” Sanatoria combined rest, diet, climate, supervision, and ideology, while admission depended on referrals, categories, beds, and budgets. NEP brought more flexible financing. The achievement expanded treatment, but a Crimean address did not give every resident a seaside bed.

The 1927 Crimean earthquakes damaged southern settlements and produced recorded Black Sea waves. Instrumental stations began operating at Yalta, Feodosiia, Simferopol, and Sevastopol, improving regional observation. Better measurement was a scientific achievement, but families first encountered shaking through falling masonry, interrupted sleep, damaged homes, frightened animals, and uncertain repairs.

sections.title: Carry water, mend pipes, manage waste, and discuss toilets honestly

items.text: Yalta inherited municipal waterworks and a separate sewer system, but war brought broken crossings, leaks, inflation, and unstable tariffs. In 1921 local rules made communal water use and household pipe or sewer repair free. The decree mattered; still, water pressure, distance, maintenance, and building connections shaped what reached a kitchen.

Sevastopol's 1925 water trust confronted a network able to supply only limited daily volume. Some residents collected water from public booths, and summer shortages were acute. Repair and finance improved parts of the system, but a strategic port still rationed convenience by neighborhood. Pipes, rather stubbornly, did not repair themselves.

Simferopol opened a sewer system in 1925 with biological treatment, yet the network had not reached full capacity. That is a real sanitation milestone, not proof that every street or dwelling was connected. Sewers also required drains, pumping, treatment, workers, fees, repairs, and habits that changed more slowly than an opening ceremony.

Reviewed sources do not provide a reliable 1920 to 1930 inventory of Crimean household toilets. City sewers imply connected fixtures somewhere, while public water booths and incomplete networks imply very unequal plumbing. The card therefore does not assign flush toilets, privies, chamber pots, or waste collectors uniformly. “Unknown” is useful plumbing information.

Health campaigns urged clean homes, safe water, ventilation, washing, inspections, and disease prevention, but domestic labor and underfunded facilities limited compliance. Women and cleaners often carried the burden while officials blamed habits. Sanitation involved hauling, scrubbing, fuel, soap, drainage, and municipal work, not simply posters telling microbes to behave.

sections.title: Weigh achievements, human costs, and the false 1930 ending

items.text: International relief joined American food and medicine with aid mobilized from Turkey and other networks. Kitchens, warehouses, transport, medical supplies, translators, and local distribution saved lives, although politics shaped access and publicity. Relief deserves credit without turning catastrophe into an uplifting adventure or hiding why households had become dependent on it.

Sanatoria and Artek developed new combinations of preventive medicine, climate therapy, children's routines, and collective care. They became influential models and employed many workers. Their benefits remained selected and unequal, especially beside famine and poor rural access. Achievement is clearest when the people admitted, excluded, cooking, cleaning, and caring remain visible.

Crimean Tatar theatre, museums, archaeological fieldwork, and new earthquake stations widened cultural and scientific work. None arose from a single “civilization.” Actors, excavators, technicians, librarians, students, and audiences built them across communities, often while negotiating censorship, funding, language reform, institutional rivalry, and political danger.

The late 1920s ended much of the NEP compromise and accelerated forced collectivization, grain procurement, and campaigns against alleged kulaks. These policies cost property, livelihoods, freedom, and lives. Modernization statistics cannot cancel coercion, and later catastrophe should not be read as inevitable from every choice made in 1920.

At the 1930 seam “south-russia” disappears, yet the Crimean ASSR, its towns, villages, institutions, families, and ecological regions continue. The atlas's “white-russia” replacement blankets places far beyond Belarus and is corrected to “ussr” by 1938. This software sequence offers no historical argument about sovereignty or present-day borders.

ending.text: At 1930 the atlas removes “south-russia” and assigns Crimea, Rostov, Donbas, Odesa, Moscow, and every other tested Soviet point to “white-russia.” By 1938 those probes are “ussr.” No White government returned and Crimea did not become Belarusian. The Crimean ASSR continued inside the Russian SFSR; forced collectivization changed life without making society vanish.
